syllabus.clause: databases use a WAL plus explicit flush points, not an fsync per small update (→ Ch.20). Volatile device write caches and FUA. Tools: strace, perf, biolatency/bpftrace, device queue-depth counters.

at.step: Measured: a thousand writes, each followed by its own fsync, made exactly one thousand real fsync syscalls, confirmed directly by strace
Measured: the exact same thousand writes, flushed every fifty records plus a final flush, made twenty-one real fsync syscalls, not a thousand
Measured: the per-update version took far longer, in real wall-clock time, than the batched version, for the identical thousand writes
None of this flushing means anything if the disk itself lies about it. What does a volatile write cache actually do, and what forces it to tell the truth?

items.item: Using WAL results in a significantly reduced number of disk writes, because only the WAL file needs to be flushed to disk to guarantee that a transaction is committed, rather than every data file changed by the transaction

at.step: PostgreSQL's own documentation makes a specific claim about why a WAL helps at all. What does it actually say the WAL avoids flushing?

items.item: when the server is processing many small concurrent transactions, one fsync of the WAL file may suffice to commit many transactions

at.step: The documentation's own words: using WAL means only the WAL file needs to be flushed, rather than every data file the transaction changed, and under load one flush can cover many transactions at once

items.item: Normally, WAL buffers should be written and flushed by an XLogFlush request, which is made, for the most part, at transaction commit time to ensure that transaction records are flushed to permanent storage

items.item: Many storage devices, especially in the consumer market, come with volatile write back caches. That means the devices signal I/O completion to the operating system before data actually has hit the non-volatile storage

items.item: The REQ_FUA flag can be OR ed into the r/w flags of a bio submitted from the filesystem and will make sure that I/O completion for this request is only signaled after the data has been committed to non-volatile storage

items.item: The 1000-versus-21 fsync count is not a sampled approximation; it is the exact arithmetic of flushing every 50th write plus one final flush over 1000 writes (1000/50 = 20, plus the one trailing flush), confirmed stable across repeated runs before being asserted.
